contentHtml:
What a secure app means for an Indian business

In short: A mobile app security checklist for an Indian business has two halves. The technical half is the OWASP MASVS, eight areas from storage to privacy, plus Android's and Apple's own rules. The legal half is CERT-In's 6-hour incident reporting, the DPDP Act and its 2025 Rules, and the privacy forms Google Play and the App Store make you fill in.

This guide was checked in November 2026, against the official pages listed at the end. I am not a lawyer, and nothing here is legal advice. Where a rule has a date, I give it.

If you want the scope and cost of an app, security work included, written down before anything is built, that is what our ₹3,500 requirement analysis produces: a call with the people who would build it and a written fixed quotation and timeline (how it works). Code, cloud and credentials stay in your name. The rest of this post needs nothing from us.

The rules that apply to an app in India

First, the obligations most Indian business apps must meet.

Rules and forms that apply to a typical Indian business app

Rule or formWho issues itWhat it asks of youIn force
Cyber security directions under section 70B(6) of the IT ActCERT-InReport listed cyber incidents within 6 hours; keep ICT system logs for 180 days in IndiaIssued 28 April 2022, effective 60 days later
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023Parliament, administered by MeitYLawful processing, security safeguards, breach notice, children's data rulesThrough the Rules below
Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025MeitYNotices, security safeguards, breach intimation to the Board within 72 hoursPublished 14 November 2025; most duties apply eighteen months later
Data safety formGoogle PlayDeclare what data the app and its SDKs collect and shareNow, for every app on Play
App privacy detailsApple App StoreDeclare data collected by you and third-party partnersNow, for new apps and updates

Source: CERT-In directions of 28 April 2022 and MeitY's DPDP Rules page and Play Console Help and Apple's app privacy details page, read 16 November 2026.

The DPDP timeline trips people up. Rule 1 of the DPDP Rules says rules 3, 5 to 16, 22 and 23 come into force eighteen months after publication. With publication in November 2025, that is May 2027. Those rules include the notice, the security safeguards and the breach intimation. CERT-In's 6-hour rule, by contrast, has applied since 2022.

OWASP MASVS: the technical standard

The OWASP MASVS (Mobile Application Security Verification Standard) describes itself as "the industry standard for mobile app security." It is free and maintained in the open. Google Play's own Data safety help page refers to it: developers can pay a Google Authorized Lab to evaluate their app against OWASP's MASVS and show an independent security review badge.

MASVS splits the work into eight control groups. Here they are with OWASP's own one-line control statements.

The eight MASVS control groups and what each asks

GroupOWASP's descriptionExample control
MASVS-STORAGESecure storage of sensitive data on a device (data-at-rest)The app securely stores sensitive data
MASVS-CRYPTOCryptographic functionality used to protect sensitive dataThe app performs key management according to industry best practices
MASVS-AUTHAuthentication and authorization mechanisms used by the mobile appThe app secures sensitive operations with additional authentication
MASVS-NETWORKSecure network communication between the mobile app and remote endpoints (data-in-transit)The app secures all network traffic according to the current best practices
MASVS-PLATFORMSecure interaction with the underlying mobile platform and other installed appsThe app uses WebViews securely
MASVS-CODESecurity best practices for data processing and keeping the app up-to-dateThe app only uses software components without known vulnerabilities
MASVS-RESILIENCEResilience to reverse engineering and tampering attemptsThe app implements anti-tampering mechanisms
MASVS-PRIVACYPrivacy controls to protect user privacyThe app offers user control over their data

Source: OWASP MASVS and MASVS-STORAGE, read 16 November 2026.

Its companion, the MASTG (Mobile Application Security Testing Guide), is "a comprehensive manual for mobile app security testing and reverse engineering." MASVS says what to achieve. MASTG says how a tester checks it on Android and iOS. When you hire someone to test your app, ask which MASVS groups they tested against and get the MASTG test references in the report.

Two notes from OWASP that save money. On resilience (anti-tampering, obfuscation and the like), OWASP says "The absence of these measures does not in itself constitute a vulnerability." They matter most for apps with something to steal or cheat: payments, rewards, paid content. And on privacy, OWASP says MASVS-PRIVACY is a baseline and should never replace a proper legal assessment.

Android: what Google's own guidance says

Google's Android security tips are worth an hour of any developer's time. The points I check first on an Indian business app:

  • Storage. Files on internal storage are "accessible only to your app" by default. External storage is "globally readable and writable", so Google says to store only non-sensitive information there. Prescriptions, ID scans and invoices belong in internal storage.
  • Logs. Google says logs are a shared resource and inappropriate logging "could inadvertently leak user data to other applications." It advises against logging personal information. Debug logs that print phone numbers or OTPs are a common find.
  • Network. "Use HTTPS over HTTP anywhere that HTTPS is supported on the server", because phones often join unsecured networks such as public Wi-Fi.
  • WebViews. If the app does not directly use JavaScript in a WebView, Google says do not call setJavaScriptEnabled().
  • Exported components. A content provider meant only for your own app should be marked android:exported=false in the manifest.
  • App integrity. The Play Integrity API helps your server check that requests come from "your genuine app binary running on a genuine Android-powered device."

iOS: what Apple builds in and requires

On iOS, a lot of network security is on by default. Apple's App Transport Security page says ATS operates by default for apps linked against the iOS 9.0 SDK or later. It requires TLS 1.2 or later and perfect forward secrecy, and blocks connections that do not meet its minimum requirements.

The catch is exceptions. Apple says exceptions "reduce the security of your app", and some, including NSAllowsArbitraryLoads, require a justification when you submit to the App Store and may trigger extra review. If a developer has switched ATS off "just to make the API work", fix the server instead.

Apple also asks about data. Its app privacy details are "required to submit new apps and app updates", and cover your third-party partners too: "analytics tools, advertising networks, third-party SDKs." Apple adds that you are "responsible for keeping your responses accurate and up to date." A privacy manifest file (PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy) records the data types an app or SDK collects and the reasons it uses certain APIs. Each SDK can ship its own.

CERT-In: the 6-hour rule

On 28 April 2022, CERT-In issued directions under section 70B(6) of the IT Act. They apply to "service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporate and Government organisations", and in my reading a company running an app is a body corporate. The parts that matter for an app owner:

  • Report within 6 hours. Incidents of the types listed in Annexure I must be reported "within 6 hours of noticing such incidents or being brought to notice about such incidents." The directions give incident@cert-in.org.in, phone 1800-11-4949 and fax 1800-11-6969.
  • Keep logs for 180 days, in India. Logs of all ICT systems must be enabled and kept securely "for a rolling period of 180 days" within Indian jurisdiction.
  • Synchronise clocks. Systems must connect to the NTP server of the National Informatics Centre (NIC) or the National Physical Laboratory (NPL), or to servers traceable to them.
  • Name a point of contact. Each entity must designate a Point of Contact to interface with CERT-In.

Annexure I lists 20 incident types. Several fit apps directly: unauthorised access of IT systems or data, data breach, data leak, attacks on applications such as e-commerce, attacks or incidents affecting digital payment systems, attacks through malicious mobile apps, fake mobile apps, and unauthorised access to social media accounts.

Two of those surprise owners. A fake copy of your app on a third-party APK site is itself reportable. And a data leak counts, not only a hack: a public cloud bucket of customer files is enough.

DPDP Act and Rules: what an app must do

The DPDP Act, 2023 is India's personal data law, and the DPDP Rules, 2025 fill in the detail. PIB's release of 14 November 2025 describes an "18-month phased compliance timeline." Here is what lands on an app.

A plain notice. Rule 3 requires an itemised description of the personal data and the specific purpose, and a link to the website or app where the person can withdraw consent "with the ease of doing so being comparable to that with which such consent was given." If sign-up is one tap, withdrawing cannot be an email to a lawyer.

Security safeguards. Rule 6 lists the minimum: encryption, obfuscation, masking or virtual tokens; access control; logs, monitoring and review to detect unauthorised access; backups to keep running after a compromise; keeping those logs and personal data for one year unless another law says otherwise; and security terms in contracts with your data processors, which includes your app developer and cloud provider.

Breach notice. Rule 7 says that on becoming aware of a personal data breach you must tell each affected person "without delay", in plain language, what happened, what it means for them and what they can do. You must tell the Data Protection Board without delay, and send a detailed report "within seventy-two hours of becoming aware of the breach", unless the Board allows longer.

Children. The Act defines a child as someone who has not completed the age of eighteen years. Section 9 requires "verifiable consent of the parent" before processing a child's data, and bans "tracking or behavioural monitoring of children or targeted advertising directed at children."

Requests. PIB's release says Data Fiduciaries must respond to people's requests "within a maximum of 90 days."

Maximum penalties in the DPDP Act Schedule that touch app security

BreachPenalty may extend to
Failing to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach₹250 crore
Failing to notify the Board or affected people of a breach₹200 crore
Failing the additional obligations for children₹200 crore
Breaching any other provision of the Act or Rules₹50 crore

Source: the Schedule to the DPDP Act, 2023, read 16 November 2026.

Google Play's Data safety form and account deletion

Play's Data safety help page says every developer with an app on Google Play must complete the form, "including apps on closed, open, or production testing tracks." Only apps on internal testing tracks are exempt. Even an app that collects no user data must fill it in and link a privacy policy.

Two lines cause most of the trouble. First, the form covers SDKs: data sent "by libraries and/or SDKs used in your app" counts, whether it goes to you or a third-party server. An analytics or ads SDK you forgot about is your declaration. Second, the form asks whether all user data is "encrypted in transit." Answer that from a test, not a guess.

If Google finds a misrepresentation, it will require a fix, and apps that do not comply face "blocked updates or removal from Google Play."

If users can create an account in your app, Play's account deletion policy requires an in-app path to delete the account and its data, and a web link where people can request deletion without the app. The web link goes in the Data safety form.

Step by step: the pre-launch checklist

The order I would work through before a first release or a big update.

Step 1. Map the data. List every piece of personal data the app touches, where it is stored (phone, server, third parties) and why. Include SDKs. This list feeds the DPDP notice, the Play form and the Apple form, so do it once and well.

Step 2. Cut what you do not need. MASVS-PRIVACY-1 says the app "minimizes access to sensitive data and resources." Every permission and field you drop is one less thing to protect, declare and report.

Step 3. Check storage and logs. Nothing sensitive on Android external storage, nothing personal in logs, secrets kept in the platform's secure storage rather than in plain preferences or the app bundle.

Step 4. Check the network. HTTPS everywhere, no ATS exceptions on iOS without a written reason, and a server that rejects old TLS versions.

Step 5. Check the server, not only the app. Change the user or order ID in a request and confirm the API refuses. Every request should check who is asking.

Step 6. Set up logs, clocks and a contact. Server and admin logs kept for at least 180 days in India for CERT-In, clocks synced to NIC or NPL, and a named person who will report an incident.

Step 7. Write the incident plan on one page. Who decides it is an incident, who emails CERT-In within 6 hours, who tells customers, and from May 2027 who reports to the Data Protection Board.

Step 8. Fill in the store forms from Step 1. Data safety on Play, app privacy details on the App Store, account deletion inside the app and on the web.

Step 9. Get an outside test if the app holds health, money or children's data. Ask for MASVS groups tested and MASTG references in the report.

Three worked examples

These are illustrative businesses, made up to show how the checklist changes by type. They are not real clients.

A clinic booking app

A clinic chain's app books appointments and lets patients download lab reports and prescriptions. The sensitive part is the files. Reports should sit in internal storage on the phone and behind per-patient access checks on the server, with download links that expire.

The CERT-In list includes data leak, so a wrongly shared report folder is reportable within 6 hours. Health data is where I would pay for an outside MASVS test before launch. More on these apps on our healthcare appointments page.

A D2C brand app with UPI and card payments

A D2C brand app takes orders and payments and sends offers. The highest-value targets are the payment flow and the account. I would keep card and UPI handling inside the payment gateway's own SDK, never storing payment details in the app, and add MASVS-AUTH-3's "additional authentication" before changing a saved address or phone number.

Attacks affecting digital payment systems are on CERT-In's list. So are fake mobile apps. Our post on payment gateway pitfalls covers the integration side.

A coaching institute app

A coaching institute app has video classes, tests and a parent login. Most students are under eighteen, so under the DPDP Act they are children. That means verifiable parental consent before processing their data, and no tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising aimed at them.

In practice: no ads SDK in the student app, analytics limited to what the institute needs to run classes, and a parent-confirmed sign-up. Paid content is also worth protecting, so this is one of the cases where MASVS-RESILIENCE controls earn their cost.

Common mistakes I see

Treating the app as the whole system. The phone is half of it. The API, the admin panel and the cloud storage hold most of the data.

Forgetting SDKs. Play and Apple both make you answer for third-party code. An old analytics SDK can make your Data safety form wrong.

No one owns the 6 hours. If nobody is named, the clock runs out while people decide whose job it is.

Logs that are either missing or full of personal data. CERT-In wants logs kept; Android's guidance wants personal data kept out of them. You need both.

Code and credentials in the developer's name. If the cloud account and store listings belong to an agency, you cannot act fast in an incident. Keep them in your company's name.

Waiting for May 2027. The DPDP duties phase in, but the work takes months, and CERT-In applies now. Our post on security basics for startups covers the server side.

A quarterly security routine

Once the app is live, one hour a quarter keeps the checklist true.

A quarterly hour for app security

TimeWhat to checkWhat you write down
First 15 minutesSDK and library list against the last release; any new ones?Changes that affect the Play and Apple privacy forms
Next 15 minutesLogs: still on, kept 180 days, no personal data creeping inAny gap, and who fixes it
Next 15 minutesIncident plan: names and numbers still correctThe current CERT-In point of contact
Last 15 minutesSearch APK sites and stores for copies of your appAny fake app, and whether it was reported

Source: CERT-In directions and Play Data safety help, read 16 November 2026.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best mobile app security checklist to follow?

OWASP MASVS is the standard most testers use, and Google Play refers to it for its independent security review. Pair it with Android's and Apple's own guidance, then add the Indian rules: CERT-In's 6-hour reporting and the DPDP Act and Rules.

Does CERT-In's 6-hour rule apply to a small business?

The 28 April 2022 directions apply to service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporate and government organisations. In my reading, a company running an app is a body corporate. If an incident of a listed type happens, it must be reported within 6 hours of noticing it.

When do the DPDP Rules apply to my app?

The Rules were published in November 2025. Rule 1 says the rules on notice, security safeguards and breach intimation come into force eighteen months after publication, which is May 2027. Plan the work now, because it touches design, contracts and logging.

Do I need to fill in Google Play's Data safety form if my app collects no data?

Yes. Play's help page says even developers whose apps collect no user data must complete the form and link a privacy policy. Only apps active solely on internal testing tracks are exempt.

Is code obfuscation required?

Not by MASVS on its own. OWASP says the absence of resilience measures does not in itself constitute a vulnerability. They are worth adding for apps with payments, paid content or anything worth cheating, after the basics are done.

What does the DPDP Act say about apps used by children?

A child is anyone under eighteen. You need verifiable consent from a parent or lawful guardian before processing a child's data, and you must not track, behaviourally monitor or target ads at children. The penalty for breaking the children's obligations may extend to ₹200 crore.

How much does a mobile app security test cost in India?

I could not find published rates I would trust, so I have not quoted one. Ask testers for a fixed quote that names the MASVS groups covered, both platforms, the server API and a retest after fixes.
